paras: The lynching of a farm hand in Simpson County, Mississippi, took place in late August 1895, when a crowd of local men hanged an unnamed Black farm hand, about 21 years old, from a tree in the Strong River swamp near Westville. He was accused of fathering a child born to the 14-year-old daughter of a local farmer, John Mulligan. Dispatches from Jackson ran in at least thirteen white newspapers across the country, some of them treating the case as unusual or questioning the father's conduct, while no Black newspaper account has been found.

According to the Jackson dispatches, Mulligan was a 'prosperous farmer' living about twenty miles southeast of Jackson, near Westville. The Savannah Morning News version said he 'compelled' his daughter to work in the fields alongside Black hands, and the Maysville dispatch said she had been 'reared in ignorance.' When she became pregnant, by this account, she first named a neighbor's son as the father. On Sunday, August 25, she gave birth to a child the papers described as black, and she then named one of the Black farm hands, who fled to the woods or swamps.

The farm hand was pursued and captured. Three dispatches, including one based on the account of J. McLeod of Simpson County, said he was first lodged in jail at Westville (printed 'Oustville' in two papers). The Maysville dispatch said that on Thursday, August 29, he was taken from the jail to be carried before a justice of the peace for a preliminary hearing, 'but he never got there.' Mulligan's neighbors met the officers in the Strong River swamp, took the prisoner and hanged him from 'the highest limb they could reach.'

Other versions of the Jackson wire omit the jail and say a 'large crowd of men and boys' or 'indignant citizens' caught him in the swamp and hanged him directly. The Savannah version added that the crowd riddled his body with bullets. All the fuller accounts agree that the body hung for twenty-four hours, and one says Sheriff McInnis cut it down.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official action against the crowd appears in the coverage, and none of the papers gave the victim's name.

The story reached the press through Jackson dispatches dated August 30 and 31, including a special to the Cincinnati Post and an account from a Simpson County visitor to Jackson. It appeared on August 31 in papers from Sacramento to Savannah and Indianapolis, then in condensed one-line weekly briefs into mid-September, along with German and Polish translations. Several of the briefs placed Simpson County in Missouri or Kentucky.

Headlines took different lines. The Fort Worth Gazette ran 'Mississippi Mob Takes Law in Their Own Hands' over 'Negro to Blame Is Strung Up,' treating the accusation as established. The Indianapolis Journal called it 'An Exceptional Case,' a hanging 'for Unusual Cause,' and the Pawtucket Tribune headlined the same text 'Mississippians' Excuse For a Lynching.' The Birmingham Age-Herald, printing the Savannah text, headlined it 'They Didn't Hang Her Father' and called it 'A Mississippi Story That Is Shocking in Several Respects,' turning attention to the father's treatment of his daughter. No account of the case has been found in Black newspapers of August and September 1895.

The accounts disagree on whether the farm hand was taken from officers after a night in jail, as three dispatches state, or caught and hanged by the crowd in the swamp, as two shorter versions have it; the jail version, which includes a named local source, is the more detailed. The dispatches also differ on the girl's age (14, or 13 in one) and the father's first name (John, Thomas or 'A.').

reader.title: Lynching of a farm hand in Simpson County, Mississippi (1895)
bases: A crowd of local men seized a Black farm hand accused of fathering a white girl's child and hanged him from a tree (A1, A3, A4, A5).

Every account has the man hanged by a 'large crowd of men and boys', 'indignant citizens' or 'Mulligan's neighbors' without trial (A1, A2, A3, A5); three say they took him from officers on his way to a justice's court (A1, A4, A5), and the stated reason was the accusation that he fathered the child (A3, A4).

At least three distinct Jackson dispatches (a Cincinnati Post special, A1; an account from J. McLeod, A5; and the 'news reached this city' version, A3) agree that a Black farm hand was hanged by a crowd in Simpson County, though they differ on custody and detail.
